title: Kings Who Rise, Fall and Repeat
overview: This chapter tracks two kings of Judah in the south and two kings of Israel in the north, showing David's family line holding on in Jerusalem while the northern throne passes by murder.

parts.label: Abijah's short reign (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: Abijah followed his father Rehoboam's wrong ways, yet the writer says his family kept the throne for David's sake. A "lamp" here means a family line that keeps going, and the one stain named on David is his adultery with Bathsheba and his arranging the death of her husband Uriah.

parts.label: Asa cleans house (vv. 9-15)
parts.note: Asa removed idols and people tied to sex rites at shrines, though scholars debate exactly who these were. He even stripped his grandmother Maakah of her powerful role as queen mother and burned her image of the goddess Asherah, but he left the local hilltop shrines standing, even though worship was meant to center on the Jerusalem temple.

parts.label: Asa buys a foreign ally (vv. 16-24)
parts.note: When Israel's king Baasha fortified Ramah, just a few miles north of Jerusalem, to choke off travel in and out of Judah, Asa paid the king of Aram with temple and palace treasure to attack Israel from the north. It worked, and Asa reused Baasha's building stones for his own forts, though a later account of his reign in the Bible faults him for trusting a foreign king instead of God.

parts.label: Nadab murdered, family wiped out (vv. 25-32)
parts.note: Jeroboam's son Nadab kept his father's worship at the golden calf shrines and was killed by Baasha during a siege after only two years. Baasha then slaughtered Jeroboam's entire family, which the writer presents as the fulfillment of an earlier prophet's warning, while still treating Baasha himself as no better.

parts.label: Baasha repeats the pattern (vv. 33-34)
parts.note: Baasha ruled Israel from Tirzah for twenty-four years but followed the same path as Jeroboam. The writer sets up a grim cycle: the man who destroyed one bad dynasty becomes the next one.

think: Asa is praised for a lifetime of loyalty yet, under pressure, emptied the temple to pay off a foreign king; how do you weigh a person's long record against what they do in a crisis?
